title: Interpreting Language Reward Models via Contrastive Explanations

contributions.purpose: Make black-box language reward models (RMs) more transparent and trustworthy by explaining any binary response comparison an RM makes, since RMs' scalar outputs lack direct meaning and no XAI technique had been applied to them.
contributions.mechanism: Adapt the contrastive-explanation paradigm (counterfactuals/CFs and semifactuals/SFs) to RM binary comparisons; a two-step attribute-conditioned LLM prompting strategy (GPT-4o) generates 15 perturbed responses per side, each modifying one of 15 high-level evaluation attributes (helpfulness, harmlessness, correctness, verbosity, etc.), then categorizes each as CF (preference flips) or SF (preference stays). Post hoc, local, model-agnostic, black-box.
contributions.evaluation: Quantitative eval on 3 open-source human-preference datasets (harmless, helpful, hs2), 3 OpenAssistant RMs (DeBERTa-large v1 0.4B, DeBERTa-large-v2, pythia-1.4b), 150 test comparisons; vs two baselines (Polyjuice, random GPT-4o perturbation). Finds CFs for both responses in >68% of inputs (harmless/helpful) and >33% (hs2) vs <=26% for baselines; lower (better) syntactic/semantic distances to originals.
contributions.source_quote: We are the first to propose contrastive explanations of binary comparisons made by RMs.

contributions.purpose: Turn local explanations into generalized, actionable insight about RM behaviour and enable comparison across RMs.
contributions.mechanism: Aggregate CFs/SFs over many comparisons to compute each attribute's Preference Flip Rate (PFR) as a global sensitivity measure; rank attributes per RM and compare RMs via Kendall's tau over ranking vectors; a workflow extracts representative examples matching an RM's global behaviour.
contributions.evaluation: On 500 comparisons/dataset (filtered to where all three RMs agree): PFR profiles (Figure 3) show that global sensitivity rankings across RMs are often similar in order but differ in magnitude (e.g. on hs2 the pythia RM is much more sensitive along every attribute).
contributions.source_quote: We demonstrate the qualitative usefulness of our method for explaining RM preferences. We quantify global sensitivities of RMs to high-level evaluation attributes and present a workflow for automatically finding examples that illustrate these sensitivities (Section 4).

self_declared_provenance.quote: In the case of RMs, the fundamental prediction task is to output rewards for two responses ... Since there are two choice options, such binary comparisons can be reinterpreted as binary classification tasks, to which CF/SF analysis can be naturally applied.
self_declared_provenance.section: introduction (adapting counterfactual/semifactual XAI, Wachter et al. 2017 / Kenny & Keane 2021, to RMs)

self_declared_provenance.quote: The approach is related to recent work on decomposing reward signals into multiple attributes ... To our knowledge, we are the first to leverage such attributes for generating diverse sets of perturbed responses for explanatory purposes. Our list of 15 attributes is partly constructed from ones used in these prior works (Zeng et al. 2024; Park et al. 2024), combined with others identified by prompting LLMs.

notes: Trade-off reported: the method's perturbations are LESS semantically diverse than the baselines (an acknowledged consequence of staying closer to the original response); authors argue attribute-grounding still yields diversity of change. Perturbation quality is sensitive to the choice of generator LLM (they pick the best-performing one). Method is descriptive/diagnostic, not a fix to RMs. Paper decision: accept.
